name: Mecasermin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2005 for a rare growth disorder, based on pooled data from five studies in 71 children, mostly open-label, in which growth speed nearly tripled in the first year. Long-term follow-up and a European registry have since confirmed the height gains.
summary: A lab-made copy of the growth factor IGF-1, approved for children who stay very short because their bodies cannot respond to growth hormone.
keyTakeaway: Mecasermin is recombinant human IGF-1, the growth factor that growth hormone normally tells the liver to make. Sold as Increlex, it was approved in 2005 for children aged 2 and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, such as Laron syndrome, whose growth hormone works but their bodies cannot respond. In the pooled studies, growth speed rose from 2.8 to 8.0 cm a year in the first year. Low blood sugar is the main risk, reported by 42% of trial children. It is not a substitute for growth hormone and is not approved for adults.

atGlance.value: Replaces missing IGF-1, which acts on growth plate cartilage to lengthen bones

atGlance.value: Injection under the skin twice a day, shortly before or after a meal or snack

blocks.text: Mecasermin is a recombinant (lab-made) form of human insulin-like growth factor-1, or IGF-1. It is a chain of 70 amino acids with three internal bridges, identical in sequence to the IGF-1 the body makes, and it is produced by E. coli bacteria that carry the human IGF-1 gene [1].

It is sold as Increlex, an injection for children with a rare cause of short stature [1]. It is a different product from IGF-1 LR3 and other modified IGF-1 versions sold online as research chemicals, which are not approved drugs and are covered separately.

Children with growth hormone insensitivity make plenty of growth hormone, but a defect in the hormone's receptor or signaling means their bodies do not respond to it, so IGF-1 stays low and they grow very slowly. Extra growth hormone cannot fix that [2]. Researchers began giving these children recombinant IGF-1 directly, and a collaborative study group followed 76 of them for up to 12 years [2].

Label adds a warning on slipped capital femoral epiphysis, a hip growth plate injury [1]

blocks.text: Normally, growth hormone binds receptors in the liver and other tissues, which then make IGF-1. IGF-1 in turn activates the type 1 IGF receptor, a close relative of the insulin receptor, on target cells [1]. At the growth plates near the ends of long bones, this drives cartilage cells to divide and then harden into bone, which lengthens the skeleton until the plates fuse after puberty [1].

Mecasermin skips the broken step. Instead of relying on a growth hormone signal the child cannot answer, it supplies IGF-1 directly [1]. Because IGF-1 also lowers blood sugar, by cutting the liver's glucose output and pushing tissues to take up glucose, the drug can cause hypoglycemia, which is why doses are timed around a meal or snack [1]. In children with severe deficiency, the half-life after an injection under the skin was about 5.8 hours [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Increlex on August 30, 2005, and it remains on the market as a prescription product [3]. The current label, revised in July 2025, lists Eton Pharmaceuticals as the manufacturer [1].

The approval is narrow. Severe primary IGF-1 deficiency is defined by a height score and a baseline IGF-1 score both at least three standard deviations below average, with normal or high growth hormone [1]. The label states that mecasermin is not a substitute for growth hormone and is not for IGF-1 deficiency caused by growth hormone deficiency, malnutrition, an underactive thyroid, or long-term steroid treatment [1]. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 2 [1].

It is prescribed for children aged 2 and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, or with a deletion of the growth hormone gene who have developed antibodies that neutralize growth hormone treatment [1]. Most children in the approval studies had Laron syndrome, the most severe form, caused by defects in the growth hormone receptor gene [1][4].

The FDA pooled five studies, four open-label and one placebo-controlled, covering 71 children who received 0.06 to 0.12 mg/kg twice daily [1]. Before treatment they averaged 6.7 years old, grew 2.8 cm a year, and stood more than six standard deviations below average height [1].

The biggest jump comes in the first year, with smaller gains afterward [2]. The long-term US cohort found the response depended on dose and stayed above baseline for up to eight years [2]. Data from 346 children in a European and US registry confirm that most gain height, and that starting younger predicts a better response [4].

Low blood sugar is the most common problem. In the approval studies, 42% of children had at least one episode, five had severe episodes needing help, and four had seizures or lost consciousness [1]. Episodes were most frequent in the first month and in younger children, and were generally avoided when the child ate within about 20 minutes of the injection [1].

items: Enlarged tonsils in 15%, sometimes needing surgery [1]
Fat lumps at injection sites (lipohypertrophy) and bruising [1]
Ear fluid, ear infections, and hearing changes [1]
Raised pressure inside the skull in three children [1]
Slipped hip growth plate and worsening of existing scoliosis [1]
Rare severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis [1]

blocks.text: Cancers have been reported after marketing in children treated with Increlex, mostly in those with genetic conditions that already raise cancer risk or who received higher than recommended doses; whether the drug caused them is unknown [1]. It is not used in children with active cancer or once the growth plates have closed, and because it contains benzyl alcohol it is not recommended for infants [1].
